title: Subobject Lattices Generators and the Grothendieck Axioms

items.title: Modular lattice
The join of two subobjects in an abelian category
The join of two subobjects is their least upper bound
items.strategy: Represent the two subobjects by monomorphisms into a common object A, form the induced map from their biproduct to A, and use the image factorization. The image contains both representatives, and the least-subobject characterization of images shows that any common upper bound factors through it.

items.title: The meet of two subobjects is their pullback
items.strategy: Pull back the two monomorphisms into A. The pullback leg is monic, so it represents a subobject of A. Its universal property makes it a lower bound, and any other lower bound factors uniquely through the pullback, making it the greatest one.

items.title: The subobjects of an object in an abelian category form a lattice
items.strategy: Use items 3 and 4 to supply binary joins and meets in the subobject poset. The zero monomorphism into A gives the bottom element and the identity of A gives the top element.

items.title: The subobject lattice of an abelian category is modular
items.strategy: Identify each interval [B1, B2] in Sub(C) with the subobject lattice of the quotient B2/B1 via the third isomorphism theorem, then use the interval-complement criterion for modularity recorded in the source notes. The point of the proof is that modularity is derived from abelian-category quotient calculus, not assumed as a lattice axiom.

items.title: The published subgroup modular law is the group instance
items.strategy: Record that the library already proves Dedekind's modular law for subgroups and that item 6 is the categorical statement of which the group theorem is an instance. Do not restate the group proof.

items.title: A subobject lattice of an abelian category need not be distributive
items.strategy: Work in Ab with $A=(\mathbb Z/2)\oplus(\mathbb Z/2)$ and let $L_1,L_2,L_3$ be its three nonzero proper subobjects. Then $L_i\wedge L_j=0$ and $L_i\vee L_j=A$ for $i\neq j$, so $$L_1\wedge(L_2\vee L_3)=L_1\neq 0=(L_1\wedge L_2)\vee(L_1\wedge L_3).$$ Thus the subobject lattice is the diamond $M_3$ and is not distributive.

items.title: Second isomorphism theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Let B and C be subobjects of A. Compare the quotient map B -> A/C with its image in A/C. Its kernel is B ∧ C, its image is the image of B in the quotient, and that image is represented by (B ∨ C)/C. The first isomorphism theorem then yields the canonical isomorphism.

items.title: Direct and inverse image of a subobject
Direct and inverse image of subobjects form a Galois connection
items.strategy: Unpack the definitions. A factorization of the direct image f_*B through C is equivalent, by the image universal property, to a factorization of B through the pullback f^*C; conversely the pullback factorization composes to give the direct-image factorization. This is exactly the adjunction inequality f_*B <= C iff B <= f^*C.

items.title: Inverse image preserves meets and direct image preserves joins
items.strategy: Apply the general order-theoretic fact that right adjoints preserve limits and left adjoints preserve colimits in posets to the Galois connection of item 11. Keep the proof at the level of lattice operations rather than repeating a pullback or image computation.

items.title: Kernel and image are inverse and direct images along a morphism
items.strategy: The pullback of the zero subobject along f is exactly the kernel of f, while the image of the identity subobject of the source along f is exactly the ordinary image of f. This lets later pages move between image-kernel language and subobject-language without a second argument.

items.title: Simple object
Composition series and composition factors of an object
Zassenhaus butterfly lemma in an abelian category
items.strategy: Form the usual butterfly from pairs of subobjects in a common ambient object. Use modular-lattice interval comparisons for the refinement pattern, then identify the relevant interval factors as quotient objects via item 9 and the third isomorphism theorem. This keeps the proof honestly split between lattice structure and quotient identification.

items.title: Schreier refinement theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Run the standard modular-lattice refinement argument for two finite subobject chains, using item 16 to identify the corresponding refined factors up to isomorphism. The theorem is stated for arbitrary finite subobject chains, not only composition series.

items.title: Jordan-Hölder theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Apply Schreier refinement to two composition series. Because each factor is simple, an equivalent refinement can only repeat the original factors up to permutation and isomorphism, so both length and factor multiset are determined.

items.title: Object of finite length
Length is additive along a subobject
items.strategy: Given B <= A, concatenate a composition series for B with the pullback of a composition series for A/B along the quotient map A -> A/B. Items 9 and 18 identify the factors and show that the resulting chain in A is a composition series, so the lengths add.

items.title: Objects of finite length form an abelian subcategory
items.strategy: Show first that subobjects and quotients of a finite-length object inherit finite composition series by restriction and quotienting. Then use item 19a to prove the extension clause: if B and A/B have finite length, the concatenated chain in A has finite length as well. The result is stated as closure under kernels, cokernels, and biproducts inside the ambient abelian category.

items.title: The published group composition-series development is the instance
items.strategy: Record that the group page already contains the subgroup versions of the butterfly, Schreier, and Jordan-Hölder theorems together with the group definition of composition length. The categorical page cites them as instances and does not reopen the group proofs.

items.title: Generator and cogenerator of a category
The axioms AB3 and AB3*
The cancellation and epimorphism descriptions of a generator agree
items.strategy: Assume AB3 so that the coproduct over Hom(G, A) exists. If G is a generator, form the canonical map from that coproduct to A and show its cokernel must vanish, since any nonzero quotient would admit a map from G contradicting the construction. Conversely, if every such canonical map is epic, then unequal morphisms are separated after precomposition by a map from G.

items.title: A locally small abelian category with a generator is well-powered
items.strategy: For a subobject A' -> A, identify Hom(G, A') with its image inside Hom(G, A). If two subobjects induce the same subset, the generator property forces them to coincide. Since Hom(G, A) is a set, the set of its subsets bounds the subobjects of A.

items.title: Generator, separator, and the three inequivalent-looking definitions
items.strategy: Record that the library's definition is the separating one from the adjoint-functor page, while Grothendieck and the Stacks Project use the subobject form and Freyd the faithfulness of Hom(G,-). Item 23 is exactly the theorem that reconciles them under the stated cocompleteness hypothesis, so the remark is convention bookkeeping rather than a second proof.

items.title: A cocomplete locally small abelian category with a generator satisfies the SAFT hypotheses dually, once representatives are supplied
items.strategy: Item 24 gives well-poweredness, while the kernel-cokernel anti-isomorphism between subobjects and quotient objects transfers this to co-well-poweredness. The generator supplies the separating side through item 22. The only extra datum named explicitly is a chosen representative family for each set of subobject classes when intersections are invoked.

items.title: A generator detects equality of subobjects
items.strategy: If B <= C then factorization through B obviously implies factorization through C. Conversely, if B is not below C, then B ∧ C is a proper subobject of B. Applying the generator property inside B yields a map from G to B that does not factor through B ∧ C, hence after composing into A it factors through B but not through C.

items.title: The axioms AB4 and AB4*
The axioms AB5 and AB5*
AB5 implies AB4
items.strategy: Apply AB5 to the directed family of finite partial coproduct images inside a coproduct of monomorphisms. Intersecting that directed join with any summand reduces to the same summand, forcing the coproduct map itself to remain monic.

items.title: Grothendieck category
Module categories are Grothendieck categories
items.strategy: Use the ring R as generator and item 23's canonical-epimorphism characterization. AB3 holds because R-Mod is cocomplete, and AB5 holds because filtered colimits of modules are computed on underlying sets and preserve exactness. Package these into the definition of a Grothendieck category.

items.title: Abelian groups satisfy AB4*
items.strategy: A product of monomorphisms of abelian groups is coordinatewise injective. Therefore products preserve kernels of quotient maps in Ab, which is exactly the AB4* condition in this primitive formulation.

items.title: Abelian groups do not satisfy AB5*
items.strategy: Take A = product_{n>=1} Z, let T_n be the subgroup of sequences whose first n coordinates vanish, and let B be the direct sum of countably many copies of Z inside A. Then intersection_n T_n = 0, but T_n + B = A for every n, so (intersection_n T_n) + B = B while intersection_n(T_n + B) = A. This violates the AB5* lattice identity.

items.title: A nonzero abelian category cannot satisfy both AB5 and AB5*
items.strategy: Follow Weibel's Exercise A.4.7 route: use a countable family built from a nonzero object and compare the two exactness behaviors forced by AB5 and AB5*. If the direct proof does not close cleanly at authoring time, this item is the designated conversion point to a sourced recorded-not-proved remark naming the exercise.

items.title: The opposite of abelian groups does not satisfy AB5
items.strategy: By item 34, Ab fails AB5*. Passing to the opposite category exchanges AB5 and AB5*, so Ab^op fails AB5. State the example explicitly to make the dual failure concrete.

items.title: Projective object
Characterisations of projective objects
items.strategy: Show that exactness of Hom(P,-) is equivalent to the lifting property against epimorphisms by unpacking surjectivity on Hom sets. Then apply the lifting property to the identity on P to characterize projectives by splitting every epimorphism onto P.

items.title: Injective object
Characterisations of injective objects
items.strategy: Pass item 37 to the opposite abelian category. The extension property against monomorphisms, exactness of Hom(-,I), and splitting of every monomorphism out of I are exactly the dual statements.

items.title: A coproduct of projectives is projective, and a product of injectives is injective
items.strategy: For a family of projectives, a map from the coproduct is the same as a family of maps from each summand; choose lifts componentwise across the target epimorphism and assemble them. Dualize in the opposite category for injectives and record that the arbitrary-family case uses one chosen lift or extension per index.

items.title: A direct summand of a projective is projective
items.strategy: If P = Q ⊕ Q' is projective and an epimorphism targets Q, precompose with the split inclusion Q -> P, lift across the epimorphism using projectivity of P, and postcompose with the split retraction P -> Q. The composite is the required lift for Q.

items.title: A category with enough projectives and enough injectives
Module categories have enough projectives
items.strategy: Every module is a quotient of a free module, and free modules are projective. Combine the published quotient theorem with the projective-module characterisation to package the result at the level of the ambient category R-Mod.

items.title: Module categories have enough injectives is already published
items.strategy: Cite the published enough-injectives and Baer-criterion theorems for modules, and record explicitly that this page does not claim the deeper theorem that every Grothendieck category has enough injectives.

items.title: A projective generator detects isomorphisms
items.strategy: Because P is a generator, Hom(P,-) is faithful; because P is projective, Hom(P,-) is exact. If Hom(P,f) is an isomorphism, exactness forces Hom(P,ker f) = 0 = Hom(P,coker f), and faithfulness forces ker f = 0 = coker f. Hence f is both monic and epic and therefore an isomorphism in an abelian category.

items.title: FALSE: the subobject lattice of an abelian category is distributive
items.strategy: Refute the statement with item 8's diamond subobject lattice in (Z/2) ⊕ (Z/2). The refutation should also say explicitly that modularity from item 6 is weaker than distributivity.

items.title: FALSE: every abelian category has a generator
items.strategy: Refute the statement with the abelian category of finite abelian groups. Any single finite abelian group has bounded exponent and only finitely many prime divisors, so it cannot separate all morphisms involving cyclic groups of unrelated prime-power order. The point is that the generator hypothesis in item 31 is a genuine size condition.

items.title: FALSE: every object of an abelian category has a composition series
items.strategy: Use Z in Ab. Its only nonzero subobjects are nZ, none of whose quotients yield a finite composition series beginning at 0, so the statement fails even in the basic module example.

items.title: FALSE: AB4 implies AB5
items.strategy: The positive implication on this page is AB5 => AB4, not the converse. Refute the converse with a verified witness at authoring time; the scaffold keeps the statement present so that the proof must either supply the witness or convert this row into a sourced remark naming the failure.

items.title: FALSE: a generator is the same thing as a projective generator
items.strategy: Refute the statement in Ab by taking Z ⊕ Z/p. It is a generator because it contains Z as a summand, but it is not projective because the Z/p summand is not. This separates the generator and projective hypotheses used together in item 44.

items.title: FALSE: Jordan-Hölder needs only a finiteness hypothesis on the category
items.strategy: Refute the statement by contrasting a finite-length object with Z in the same abelian category Ab. The hypothesis that matters is on the object having a composition series, exactly as items 18 and 19 state.

title: Subobject Lattices Generators and the Grothendieck Axioms — Examples

items.title: The subobject lattice of a cyclic group of order twelve
items.strategy: Identify subgroups of C12 with divisors of 12. The example exhibits explicitly how meet, join, and modularity reduce to gcd and lcm in a familiar lattice that is distributive, unlike the diamond example on the A page.

items.title: The subobject lattice of a two-dimensional vector space
items.strategy: Work with a two-dimensional vector space over a field and list its zero subspace, its one-dimensional lines, and the whole space. This gives a second concrete modular-not-necessarily-distributive picture and shows how the diamond appears already in linear algebra over F2.

items.title: The Galois connection of images and preimages for a module homomorphism
items.strategy: Choose a concrete module homomorphism, compute direct images and pullback submodules on a short list of subobjects, and verify the adjunction inequality f_*B <= C iff B <= f^*C on each pair. Keep the example finite enough that the lattice operations are visible by hand.

items.title: Two composition series of a module refined
items.strategy: Pick a finite-length module with two visible composition chains, refine them explicitly, and match the simple factors. The goal is to show the Schreier and Jordan-Hölder statements as calculations rather than as abstract lattice theorems alone.

items.title: The ring as a generator of its module category
items.strategy: Show directly that maps from R into a left R-module M are in bijection with elements of M, so the canonical coproduct map from copies of R indexed by M onto M is the obvious surjection. This is the concrete content behind item 32.

items.title: The category of finite abelian groups has no nonzero projective object
items.strategy: Substitute the denied sheaf example with the abelian category of finite abelian groups. Any nonzero projective there would have a nonzero simple quotient Z/p; splitting that quotient would make Z/p projective, but the epimorphism Z/p^2 -> Z/p does not split. Hence no nonzero projective object exists.

items.title: A directed union of subgroups meeting a fixed subgroup
items.strategy: Take an increasing chain of subgroups in an abelian group and compute both sides of the AB5 lattice identity with a fixed subgroup. The example shows the directed-union form of AB5 in the concrete module case that item 32 packages abstractly.

items.title: Length computed for a finite abelian group
items.strategy: Choose a finite abelian group in invariant-factor or primary decomposition form, write a composition series explicitly, and compute its length as the total multiplicity of simple p-primary factors. Then verify item 19a on a visible subobject.
